title: DC History and Government (12th Grade)
description: District of Columbia History and Government (12th Grade) practice - 100 questions. The required District of Columbia History and Government course, DC Social Studies Standards (2023) DC.1-DC.51: early settlement and geography 1400-1790; birth of the nation's capital 1790-1865; emergence of modern DC 1865-1968; self-determination 1968-1998; contemporary DC 1998-present, with the grade-8 Action Civics DC layer carried at assessed depth.

questions.question: The Indigenous people whose principal town, Nacotchtank, stood near the meeting of the Potomac and Anacostia rivers were the:
questions.correctAnswer: Anacostan (Nacotchtank) people, an Algonquian-speaking community
distractors: Powhatan paramount chief's own royal household
Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) longhouse confederacy
Spanish mission community from Florida
questions.explanation: Nacotchtank was a thriving Anacostan trading town at the confluence of the two rivers. Its people were Algonquian speakers linked by trade and kinship to the Piscataway paramountcy to the south.
questions.memoryHook: Start where the two rivers meet - Nacotchtank.

img.tip: Start where the two rivers meet - Nacotchtank.
img.title: WHERE TWO RIVERS MEET

questions.question: The Anacostan and their neighbors the Piscataway belonged to which language and culture family?
questions.correctAnswer: Algonquian
distractors: Siouan
Iroquoian
Muskogean
questions.explanation: Both peoples spoke Algonquian languages, the family shared by most Indigenous nations of the Chesapeake and mid-Atlantic coast. Their towns farmed corn, beans and squash and traded widely by river.
questions.memoryHook: Algonquian voices along the rivers.

img.scene: A forest riverbank with a garden of corn, beans and squash and a village path leading to the water. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Algonquian voices along the rivers.
img.title: ALGONQUIAN HOMELANDS

questions.question: Why was the site of today's Washington so well suited to Indigenous trade?
questions.correctAnswer: It sat at the fall line where the Potomac met the Anacostia, linking coastal trade with inland peoples
distractors: It had the deepest ocean harbor on the Atlantic coast
It stood beside a gold-bearing mountain range
It was an island protected on every side by cliffs
questions.explanation: The fall line - where the Piedmont drops to the coastal plain - forced river travelers to stop and portage, making the confluence a natural exchange point between coastal and interior nations.
questions.memoryHook: The fall line made traders stop - and meet.

img.scene: A rocky river rapid at the edge of wooded hills with canoes pulled ashore and bundles of trade goods on the bank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The fall line made traders stop - and meet.
img.title: THE FALL LINE CROSSROADS

questions.question: Archaeological evidence from sites along the Anacostia shows Indigenous people used this area for thousands of years mainly to:
questions.correctAnswer: Hunt, fish, gather and quarry tool stone in seasonal rounds
distractors: Mine silver for export to Europe
Operate ocean-going sailing ships
Build permanent stone cities of many thousands
questions.explanation: Dig sites along the Anacostia have uncovered quartz and quartzite tool-making debris, pottery and camp remains spanning thousands of years - evidence of rich seasonal hunting, fishing and quarrying grounds rather than one single permanent city.
questions.memoryHook: Stone tools tell the longest story here.

img.scene: An archaeologist's careful grid excavation beside a river, stone flakes and pottery fragments laid out on a cloth. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Stone tools tell the longest story here.
img.title: EVIDENCE IN THE EARTH

questions.question: When Captain John Smith explored the Potomac River in 1608, he found the Nacotchtank community:
questions.correctAnswer: Prospering as a center of trade in furs and goods from distant peoples
distractors: Abandoned and empty after a recent war
Already converted to a Spanish mission
Ruled directly from the Powhatan capital as a fort
questions.explanation: Smith's 1608 voyage recorded Nacotchtank as a well-supplied trading hub receiving goods - including items from peoples far inland - which is why later English traders followed the same river routes.
questions.memoryHook: Smith found a marketplace, not a wilderness.

img.scene: Sailing shallops with furled sails approaching a busy riverbank village, crews trading cloth and tools for furs. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Smith found a marketplace, not a wilderness.
img.title: 1608: THE TRADING TOWN

questions.question: In the century after European contact, the Anacostan and Piscataway populations collapsed mainly because of:
questions.correctAnswer: European diseases, land loss and colonial violence and displacement
distractors: A volcanic eruption that buried their towns
Their decision to migrate together to Canada
A drought that ended all farming in the region
questions.explanation: Epidemics of smallpox and other introduced diseases, settler seizure of riverfront farmland, and colonial wars shattered both peoples. Survivors consolidated with the Piscataway or other nations; their descendants, including the Piscataway Indian Nation, remain in Maryland today.
questions.memoryHook: Disease and dispossession, not disappearance.

img.scene: An empty village clearing at dusk with a few standing houses and an overgrown garden, a river flowing quietly beyond. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Disease and dispossession, not disappearance.
img.title: A QUIETED VILLAGE

questions.question: The land that became the District of Columbia was, in the colonial period, part of which colony?
questions.correctAnswer: Maryland on the eastern side of the Potomac and Virginia on the western side
distractors: Pennsylvania on both sides of the river
North Carolina
Delaware
questions.explanation: The future district straddled the Potomac: the Maryland shore (chartered 1632, with land granted to planters such as Daniel Carroll and Notley Young) and the Virginia shore around Alexandria. Georgetown (1751) and Alexandria (1749) were colonial tobacco ports before the capital existed.
questions.memoryHook: Two colonies faced each other across the river.

img.scene: Two colonial tobacco ports with wooden wharves and sailing ships facing each other across a wide river. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Two colonies faced each other across the river.
img.title: TOBACCO PORTS

questions.question: Georgetown and Alexandria grew wealthy before the capital arrived chiefly by exporting which crop?
questions.correctAnswer: Tobacco
distractors: Cotton
Coffee
Silk
questions.explanation: Both ports shipped Maryland and Virginia tobacco to Europe and imported finished goods in return. Their wharves, warehouses and merchants were the commercial base the new federal city grew beside.
questions.memoryHook: Tobacco paid for the wharves.

img.scene: Workers rolling large wooden hogshead barrels down a wharf toward a tall sailing ship at a colonial port. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Tobacco paid for the wharves.
img.title: TOBACCO WHARVES

questions.question: Colonial farms on the future district's land depended heavily on the labor of:
questions.correctAnswer: Enslaved Africans and African Americans
distractors: Wage workers recruited from New England
Indentured servants only, for the whole period
Prisoners sent from English jails
questions.explanation: By the mid-1700s enslaved people did much of the tobacco fieldwork and skilled labor on the plantations and in the ports of the area - a founding fact of the district's history that the standards require students to confront directly.
questions.memoryHook: Enslaved labor built the colonial economy here.

img.scene: Enslaved workers tending tobacco plants in a broad field at dawn, a plantation house distant on a hill. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Enslaved labor built the colonial economy here.
img.title: LABOR THAT BUILT THE LAND

questions.question: The Potomac River at the district falls into which larger body of water?
questions.correctAnswer: The Chesapeake Bay
distractors: The Great Lakes
The Gulf of Mexico
The Atlantic Ocean directly at the district line
questions.explanation: The Potomac flows southeast from the district past Mount Vernon and widens into the Chesapeake Bay, which connects it to Atlantic shipping - one reason a capital here could be reached by sea yet sit inland.
questions.memoryHook: Potomac to the Bay to the sea.

img.scene: A wide river widening into a broad bay with marshy shores and distant sails under a morning sky. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Potomac to the Bay to the sea.
img.title: RIVER TO BAY

questions.question: Rock Creek, which cuts through the western side of the district, mattered to early settlement because it:
questions.correctAnswer: Powered gristmills and marked a natural boundary between farms and towns
distractors: Was navigable by ocean ships to its source
Contained gold deposits that funded the city
Formed the border between Maryland and Virginia
questions.explanation: Rock Creek's falling water turned millstones at gristmills such as Peirce Mill, grinding grain for the area's farms, and its wooded valley later became one of the nation's first large urban parks (1890).
questions.memoryHook: Creek power ground the grain.

img.scene: A stone gristmill with a turning waterwheel beside a rocky wooded creek, sacks of grain stacked by the door. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Creek power ground the grain.
img.title: MILL ON ROCK CREEK

questions.question: The people called Piscataway were significant to the future district's site because they:
questions.correctAnswer: Were the paramount Algonquian power whose territory included the district's Maryland shore
distractors: Built the first stone fort on the Potomac in 1600
Signed the treaty that created the United States
Supplied the surveyors who drew the district in 1791
questions.explanation: The Piscataway paramount chief (the Tayac) held authority over towns on both sides of the lower Potomac, including the district's eastern shore; Maryland's colonial government treated with the Piscataway as the region's Indigenous sovereign.
questions.memoryHook: The Tayac's towns ringed the future capital.

img.scene: A large council gathering beside a river with a chief's longhouse, woven mats and visiting delegations arriving by canoe. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Tayac's towns ringed the future capital.
img.title: THE PISCATAWAY PARAMOUNTCY

questions.question: Which statement best describes Indigenous land use around the future district before 1790?
questions.correctAnswer: Managed landscapes of towns, cornfields, hunting forests and fishing camps held in common by kin groups
distractors: Empty wilderness with no settled communities
Fenced private farms owned by individual families
A single walled city ruled by one king
questions.explanation: Indigenous peoples actively managed this landscape - clearing fields, burning underbrush to aid hunting, and moving seasonally among towns and camps. Land was held by communities, not sold as individual property, a difference that shaped every later land conflict.
questions.memoryHook: A worked and tended homeland, not an empty one.

img.scene: A patchwork of cornfields, managed open woodland and a small village seen from a low hill at harvest time. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A worked and tended homeland, not an empty one.
img.title: A MANAGED LANDSCAPE

questions.question: European colonization changed Indigenous life in the Potomac valley first and most directly through:
questions.correctAnswer: New trade goods and diseases arriving together along the river trade routes
distractors: The building of stone churches in every town
A single treaty signed in 1492
The introduction of horses from the western plains
questions.explanation: Metal tools, cloth and guns entered through trade and were eagerly sought, but the same routes carried smallpox and other diseases ahead of settlement itself - transforming populations and power balances before most colonists arrived.
questions.memoryHook: Trade and disease traveled the same river.

img.scene: A trading scene on a riverbank with bundles of cloth and metal tools beside furs, canoes drawn up on the shore. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Trade and disease traveled the same river.
img.title: GOODS AND GERMS

questions.question: The future district's land on the Maryland side was granted by the colony mainly to:
questions.correctAnswer: Planter families who established tobacco plantations worked by enslaved labor
distractors: A mining company searching for iron ore
Religious refugees building a walled commune
The British navy as a permanent shipyard
questions.explanation: Maryland's proprietor granted tracts along the Potomac and Anacostia - to families including the Youngs, Carrolls and Burneses, the same landowners who in 1791 would convey land for the federal city.
questions.memoryHook: Plantation grants became the capital's ground.

img.scene: A surveyor with a tripod and chain measuring a tobacco field boundary beside a river, a plantation house behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Plantation grants became the capital's ground.
img.title: GRANTS ON THE RIVER

questions.question: Why does the standards' timeline for this course begin around 1400 rather than 1790?
questions.correctAnswer: Because DC history starts with the Indigenous societies and geographies that existed centuries before the capital
distractors: Because the first European city on the site was founded in 1400
Because the Constitution was drafted in 1400
Because archaeologists found a European coin dated 1400
questions.explanation: Driving concept 1 (1400-1790) deliberately seats the capital's story inside a much older Indigenous history: the standards treat Nacotchtank and Piscataway societies as the course's foundation, not a preface.
questions.memoryHook: 1790 is a chapter, not the beginning.

img.scene: Layered earth strata in an excavation wall with pottery shards in the lower layers and a distant modern skyline above. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 1790 is a chapter, not the beginning.
img.title: HISTORY BEFORE THE CAPITAL

questions.question: The Anacostia River's name preserves the memory of:
questions.correctAnswer: The Nacotchtank (Anacostan) people who lived and traded at its banks
distractors: A Spanish explorer who mapped it in 1520
The Latin word for the fall line
A colonial governor of Maryland
questions.explanation: 'Anacostia' derives from Nacotchtank, the Anacostan town at the rivers' meeting. The name survived the people's displacement - a pattern repeated in Potomac and other regional place names.
questions.memoryHook: The river still speaks their name.

img.scene: A calm river at sunrise with herons in the marsh grass and wooded banks reflected in the water. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The river still speaks their name.
img.title: THE RIVER REMEMBERS

questions.question: Which geographic feature most limited large sailing ships traveling up the Potomac toward the future district?
questions.correctAnswer: The fall line rapids above Georgetown, where the Piedmont meets the coastal plain
distractors: A permanent ice pack near Alexandria
A sandbar at the river's mouth in the bay
Waterfalls at the Anacostia's mouth
questions.explanation: Above Georgetown the river turns to rapids at Little Falls - the fall line. Ocean ships stopped at the ports below it, which fixed Georgetown and Alexandria as the colonial commercial centers.
questions.memoryHook: Ships stopped where the river fell.

img.scene: A tall ship anchored below rocky rapids while smaller boats carry cargo past the white water. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Ships stopped where the river fell.
img.title: WHERE SHIPS STOPPED

questions.question: By the 1780s, the town of Georgetown was known as a port that:
questions.correctAnswer: Exported tobacco and flour and imported European goods for the backcountry trade
distractors: Built the United States Navy's largest warships
Refused all trade with European merchants
Specialized in whaling voyages to the Arctic
questions.explanation: Georgetown's merchants graded and shipped tobacco, milled flour from backcountry wheat, and distributed imports inland - the commercial network Washington and the commissioners found already operating in 1791.
questions.memoryHook: A working port before it was a capital.

img.scene: A busy colonial wharf with flour barrels, tobacco hogsheads and merchants inspecting goods beside a warehouse. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A working port before it was a capital.
img.title: GEORGETOWN AT WORK

questions.question: The Piscataway and Anacostan experience after colonization most directly illustrates which theme of this course?
questions.correctAnswer: Indigenous peoples shaped this place first and were then displaced by colonization and slavery's expansion
distractors: Native nations voluntarily dissolved without pressure
Europeans avoided the Potomac valley entirely
Colonization ended all Indigenous presence in Maryland at once
questions.explanation: Descendant communities - including Piscataway nations in Maryland recognized today - persisted despite disease, land loss and removal pressures. The standards frame the course with both dispossession and survival.
questions.memoryHook: Displaced, not vanished.

img.scene: A modern Indigenous community gathering with drums and regalia beside a Maryland river at a summer festival. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Displaced, not vanished.
img.title: SURVIVAL AND MEMORY

questions.question: The Constitution gave Congress power over a future federal district in which clause?
questions.correctAnswer: Article I, Section 8 - Congress may exercise exclusive legislation over a district ceded by states as the seat of government
distractors: The First Amendment's assembly clause
Article II's commander-in-chief clause
The Tenth Amendment's reserved powers clause
questions.explanation: The 'Seat of Government' clause (Article I, Section 8, Clause 17) let states cede up to ten miles square for a federal district under Congress's exclusive authority - the legal root of DC's unique status and of its residents' lack of voting representation.
questions.memoryHook: One clause created a capital without voters.

img.scene: A parchment document and quill on a wooden desk with delegates' chairs arranged in a semicircle behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: One clause created a capital without voters.
img.title: THE SEAT OF GOVERNMENT CLAUSE

questions.question: The Residence Act of 1790 placed the permanent capital:
questions.correctAnswer: On the Potomac River, on land ceded by Maryland and Virginia
distractors: In New York City permanently
On the Ohio River near Pittsburgh
In Philadelphia for another fifty years
questions.explanation: After temporary seats in New York and Philadelphia, the Residence Act fixed the capital on the Potomac; President Washington chose the exact site. The government moved there in 1800.
questions.memoryHook: The Potomac won the capital.

img.scene: A president on horseback surveying a wooded riverbank with surveyors and a map spread on a camp table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Potomac won the capital.
img.title: CHOOSING THE SITE

questions.question: The choice of a Potomac capital was part of the Compromise of 1790, in which southern support was traded for:
questions.correctAnswer: Federal assumption of the states' Revolutionary War debts
distractors: Immediate abolition of slavery in Virginia
A promise to move the capital again in 20 years
Free land for every veteran in the district
questions.explanation: At the famous Jefferson-hosted bargain, Hamilton's financial plan (federal assumption of state debts) passed in exchange for a southern capital site. The deal placed the seat of government inside two slaveholding states - a fact DC.7 asks students to weigh.
questions.memoryHook: Debts for a southern capital.

img.scene: Three statesmen in 18th-century dress talking earnestly over a dinner table with maps and ledgers. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Debts for a southern capital.
img.title: THE DINNER-TABLE BARGAIN

questions.question: The original District of Columbia was shaped as:
questions.correctAnswer: A square, ten miles on each side, set at an angle like a diamond across the Potomac
distractors: A circle ten miles wide
A rectangle along only the Maryland shore
Whatever land the commissioners could buy cheaply
questions.explanation: The 1791-92 survey marked a ten-mile square - 100 square miles - rotated 45 degrees, with boundary stones placed at one-mile intervals. The Virginia portion was returned in the 1840s, leaving today's smaller district.
questions.memoryHook: A diamond drawn on two states.

img.scene: Surveyors placing a carved boundary stone in a forest clearing while a chain crew measures through the trees. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A diamond drawn on two states.
img.title: THE DIAMOND DISTRICT

questions.question: The surveyor who helped lay out the district's boundaries and is remembered as a free Black mathematician and astronomer was:
questions.correctAnswer: Benjamin Banneker
distractors: Pierre L'Enfant
Andrew Ellicott
Thomas Jefferson
questions.explanation: Banneker, a free Black Marylander and self-taught astronomer, worked with Andrew Ellicott's 1791 survey team making the astronomical observations that fixed the district's starting point at Jones Point.
questions.memoryHook: Banneker read the stars for the survey.

img.scene: An astronomer adjusting a brass telescope and clock by lantern light at a survey camp under a starry sky. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Banneker read the stars for the survey.
img.title: THE ASTRONOMER SURVEYOR

questions.question: French-born engineer Pierre Charles L'Enfant designed the capital city with:
questions.correctAnswer: Grand diagonal avenues over a street grid, with circles and squares reserving space for monuments and public buildings
distractors: Narrow winding lanes copied from medieval Paris
A single main street with all buildings facing the river
Concentric canals modeled on Amsterdam
questions.explanation: L'Enfant's 1791 plan overlaid baroque diagonal avenues on a grid, reserving prominent sites for the Capitol, the President's House and future monuments. Fired in 1792, he saw his plan revived a century later by the McMillan Plan.
questions.memoryHook: Avenues radiating like sun rays.

img.scene: In the year 1791, a French engineer in 18th-century dress unrolling a vast city plan with radiating avenues across a table overlooking a river bluff, period clothing, candles and brass instruments nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Avenues radiating like sun rays.
img.title: L'ENFANT'S VISION

questions.question: The landowners who held most of the federal city's site in 1791 - including Daniel Carroll and David Burnes - agreed to:
questions.correctAnswer: Convey land for public buildings and streets, and sell building lots whose proceeds were shared with the government
distractors: Donate all their land free of charge
Leave the district and settle in Ohio
Burn their farms rather than sell to Congress
questions.explanation: The 1791 agreement with the 'original proprietors' divided the platted lots between the owners and the United States; lot sales were supposed to finance the Capitol and President's House - and chronically fell short.
questions.memoryHook: Lot sales were meant to build a capital.

img.scene: In the year 1791, landowners and officials in 18th-century dress signing a large agreement at a table in a plantation house, farmland visible through the window, quills and wax seal on the table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Lot sales were meant to build a capital.
img.title: THE PROPRIETORS' BARGAIN

questions.question: The Organic Act of 1801 changed DC residents' political rights by:
questions.correctAnswer: Placing the district under Congress's direct control and ending residents' voting in Maryland and Virginia elections
distractors: Giving DC three voting members of Congress
Making DC a state with its own legislature
Granting the vote to all adult residents of the city
questions.explanation: When Congress assumed jurisdiction in 1801, people living in the district lost the state voting rights they had exercised as Marylanders and Virginians. The act split the district into Washington and Alexandria counties and kept Maryland/Virginia law in force - but representation was gone.
questions.memoryHook: 1801: governed, but voiceless.

img.scene: Residents in early 1800s dress standing outside a courthouse reading a posted proclamation with grave expressions. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 1801: governed, but voiceless.
img.title: RIGHTS LOST IN 1801

questions.question: Retrocession in 1846-47 returned which part of the district to Virginia?
questions.correctAnswer: The southwestern portion across the Potomac, including Alexandria
distractors: Georgetown and the land north of the Mall
The Anacostia neighborhood east of the river
No land was ever returned
questions.explanation: Alexandria's residents - citing economic neglect and fearing Congress might abolish the slave trade in the district - voted to rejoin Virginia; Congress agreed in 1846 and Virginia accepted in 1847. Today's DC is only the Maryland cession.
questions.memoryHook: The diamond lost its southern corner.

img.scene: A 19th-century river port town with a courthouse square and a steamboat landing across the river from a distant capitol dome. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The diamond lost its southern corner.
img.title: ALEXANDRIA GOES HOME

questions.question: During the War of 1812, British forces struck Washington by:
questions.correctAnswer: Defeating American defenders at Bladensburg and burning the Capitol, the President's House and other public buildings in August 1814
distractors: Capturing the city by naval blockade without landing
Buying the city from its commissioners
Occupying Georgetown for three years
questions.explanation: The 'Bladensburg Races' rout opened the road to Washington; British troops burned the public buildings on August 24, 1814. A violent storm the next day helped drive them out, and the buildings were rebuilt in place.
questions.memoryHook: 1814: the capital in flames.

img.scene: A neoclassical public building at night with smoke rising and soldiers' campfires in the street, townspeople fleeing with bundles. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 1814: the capital in flames.
img.title: THE BURNING OF WASHINGTON

questions.question: Washington's economy in the early 1800s included a nationally notorious trade in:
questions.correctAnswer: Enslaved people, sold through pens and traders in the capital itself
distractors: Gold mined in Rock Creek
Whale oil from district fisheries
Silk produced by district workshops
questions.explanation: Slave traders held enslaved people in pens within sight of the Capitol and marched coffles through the city to ships at Alexandria. Abolitionists made 'the slave trade in the capital' a national scandal; the Compromise of 1850 banned the trade (not slavery) in DC.
questions.memoryHook: Coffles marched past the Capitol.

img.scene: An enslaved coffle in chains walking a dusty road with a white domed building far in the background haze. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Coffles marched past the Capitol.
img.title: SHAME IN SIGHT OF THE CAPITOL

questions.question: The Pearl incident of 1848 was:
questions.correctAnswer: The attempted escape of 77 enslaved people aboard the schooner Pearl, the largest single escape attempt in U.S. history
distractors: A naval battle in the Potomac during the Civil War
The theft of jewels from the President's House
A flood that destroyed the Navy Yard
questions.explanation: Enslaved families boarded the Pearl in April 1848 hoping to sail to freedom; becalmed and captured, most were sold south. The attempt and the riots that followed deepened the national fight over slavery in the capital.
questions.memoryHook: Seventy-seven souls on one schooner.

img.scene: A two-masted schooner at anchor on a dark river at night with families quietly boarding from small boats. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Seventy-seven souls on one schooner.
img.title: THE PEARL

questions.question: The Compensated Emancipation Act of April 16, 1862 did what in DC?
questions.correctAnswer: Freed about 3,100 enslaved people - the only compensated emancipation in U.S. history - with payments to loyal owners
distractors: Freed all enslaved people in every state at once
Banned Black migration into the district
Restored the slave trade in Washington
questions.explanation: Congress abolished slavery in the district nine months before the Emancipation Proclamation, compensating loyal owners up to $300 per freed person. April 16 is still celebrated as DC Emancipation Day, a public holiday in the District.
questions.memoryHook: Freedom first, in the capital.

img.scene: Families celebrating in a city street in spring 1862, reading a posted proclamation, church bells in a tower behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Freedom first, in the capital.
img.title: EMANCIPATION DAY

questions.question: The 1862 emancipation law also funded:
questions.correctAnswer: Voluntary emigration (colonization) payments for freed people who chose to leave the United States
distractors: A new palace for the mayor
Pensions for former slave traders
A wall around the district
questions.explanation: The act set aside money for freed people who voluntarily emigrated to Haiti or Liberia - reflecting Lincoln-era colonization thinking that most DC Black leaders rejected, insisting their future was in America.
questions.memoryHook: Most chose to stay and claim America.

img.scene: A freed family unpacking belongings in a modest city home with books and a child's slate on the table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Most chose to stay and claim America.
img.title: STAYING TO BUILD A LIFE

questions.question: In 1867, Congress extended voting rights in DC to:
questions.correctAnswer: Black men - making DC one of the first places in the nation where Black men could vote, over President Johnson's veto
distractors: All women residents
Only property owners
Teenagers aged 16 and older
questions.explanation: Congress passed Black male suffrage for the district in January 1867, overriding Andrew Johnson's veto - three years before the Fifteenth Amendment. Black voters immediately became a decisive force in city elections.
questions.memoryHook: DC voted Black ballots in 1867.

img.scene: Black men in 1860s dress proudly casting ballots at a wooden ballot box in a crowded polling place. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: DC voted Black ballots in 1867.
img.title: FIRST BALLOTS

questions.question: The first public schools for Black children in DC were established in:
questions.correctAnswer: 1862, when Congress authorized public education for African American children in the district
distractors: 1801, with the Organic Act
1900, after Plessy's ruling
1954, with Bolling v. Sharpe
questions.explanation: Wartime Congress funded separate public schools for Black children beginning in 1862; leaders such as Myrtilla Miner had earlier run private schools for Black girls despite mob opposition. The dual school system lasted until 1954.
questions.memoryHook: School doors opened in 1862 - separately.

img.scene: A one-room 1860s schoolroom with Black children at wooden desks and a teacher at a chalkboard. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: School doors opened in 1862 - separately.
